CausalChain: CTNNB1 exon 3 mutation -> Dysregulated Wnt/β-catenin signaling -> Altered transcription of metabolic genes (CYP enzymes and glycolytic regulators) -> Metabolic reprogramming (reduced phase I activity & enhanced glycolysis) -> Impaired xenobiotic clearance and multifactorial chemoresistance -> Hepatoblastoma-like phenotype
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that in HepG2 cells, the CTNNB1 exon 3 mutation activates the Wnt/β-catenin pathway in a manner that simultaneously downregulates cytochrome P450 enzymes and upregulates key glycolytic regulators, resulting in a comprehensive metabolic reprogramming. This reprogramming reduces phase I metabolic activity and alters energy production pathways, leading to impaired xenobiotic clearance and intrinsic chemoresistance, thereby driving a hepatoblastoma-like phenotype. Using contemporary approaches—such as CRISPR-mediated gene editing to correct the CTNNB1 mutation, RNA-seq and single-cell analyses to monitor changes in metabolic gene expression, and pharmacologic modulation of Wnt signaling—we intend to dissect and potentially reverse these metabolic alterations, which could restore sensitivity to therapy.
Abstract: We propose that in HepG2 cells, the CTNNB1 exon 3 mutation triggers dysregulation of the canonical Wnt/β‐catenin pathway, which not only alters the transcriptional regulation of cytochrome P450 enzymes but also orchestrates a broader metabolic reprogramming, including enhanced glycolysis. This dual alteration impairs phase I xenobiotic metabolism and contributes to chemoresistance, thereby promoting a hepatoblastoma‐like phenotype. Leveraging state-of-the-art technologies such as CRISPR-based genome editing, high-throughput transcriptomics, and single-cell metabolic profiling, our hypothesis aims to clarify the mechanistic underpinnings of this multifaceted metabolic shift. Furthermore, we posit that precise modulation of the Wnt/β-catenin pathway can restore metabolic homeostasis, normalize xenobiotic clearance, and sensitize tumor cells to chemotherapeutic agents.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis focused narrowly on CTNNB1 exon 3 mutation-driven Wnt/β-catenin dysregulation leading to decreased cytochrome P450 activity as the sole contributor to chemoresistance. In the revised hypothesis, we broaden this view by incorporating the role of metabolic reprogramming—encompassing both diminished CYP activity and enhanced glycolysis—in the development of chemoresistance. Each causal step of the original chain is preserved but expanded: the mutation still triggers Wnt dysregulation; however, instead of solely impacting CYP enzymes, the altered signaling reprograms a broader metabolic network. Advanced molecular tools (e.g., CRISPR, RNA-seq, single-cell profiling) are invoked to provide practical interrogation and modulation of this pathway, thereby enhancing the feasibility and scientific rigor of the hypothesis.
